newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil airports boost security after plane blast.
newsitem.headline: Brazil airports boost security after plane blast.

text.p: Brazilian authorities boosted security at airports on Friday amid suspicion that a bomb might have caused an explosion on an airliner that ripped open the fuselage and sucked out a passenger.

Federal airport administrator INFRAERO said in a statement it had launched an "emergency program" to equip airports with metal detectors and X-ray equipment after Wednesday's blast on a Brazilian TAM airline Fokker-100 jet.
"From today, all the 67 airports in the network have been instructed to double security measures," INFRAERO said.
TAM Flight 283 was on a routine trip in Sao Paulo state when an explosion tore a six-foot by four-foot (two- by 1.3-metre) hole in the plane's fuselage.
A 38-year-old engineer was sucked out and fell 7,200 feet (2,400 metres) to his death.
Technicians began tests on Thursday to see whether the blast was caused by a bomb or some other explosive material.
INFRAERO said it was investing 9.65 million reais (about $9 million) to the end of 1998 to improve security equipment at its airports.

Brazil's main international airports at Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador, Brasilia and Recife have security that meets international standards. But six smaller airports have no security arrangements and 15 others are equipped only with handheld metal detectors, INFRAERO said.

The blast was the second blow in less than a year for TAM, Brazil's premier regional carrier. Eight months ago, a TAM Fokker-100 crashed in a densely populated area of Sao Paulo, killing 98 people, two of them on the ground.
TAM was voted company of the year by Exame business magazine last week.
